31. The NBFC must use Digital Signature Certificates (DSCs), to authenticate its identity electronically, and to ensure confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation of information in online transactions and important electronic documents.
32. The NBFC must undertake a comprehensive risk assessment of its IT systems at least on an annual basis.
The assessment must make an analysis on the threats and vulnerabilities to the IT assets of the NBFC and its existing security controls and processes.
The outcome of the exercise must be to find out the risks present and to determine the appropriate level of controls necessary for appropriate mitigation of risks.
The risk assessment must be brought to the notice of the CRO, CIO, and the Board of the NBFC, and must serve as an input for Information Security auditors.

33. The NBFC, if using or intending to use mobile financial services, must develop a mechanism for safeguarding information assets that are used by mobile applications to provide services to customers.
The technology used for mobile services must ensure confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and end-to-end encryption.
34. The NBFC leveraging social media platforms for product marketing must be well equipped to handle social media risks and threats including unauthorised account takeovers and impersonation fraud.
35. The NBFC must establish and implement a robust, ongoing information security training and awareness program for all users.
This program must be periodically reviewed and updated to remain aligned with evolving IT landscapes, emerging cyber threats, and the NBFC’s information security framework.
36. The NBFC must deploy a formal mechanism to measure and track the effectiveness of such training through periodic assessments or testing.
The NBFC must also maintain an up-to-date repository of the training and awareness status of all users.
37. The NBFC must process and store information in a manner that ensures availability of required information in a timely, reliable, secure, and resilient manner.

38. The NBFC must identify and assess risks associated with existing and planned IT operations, align such risks with its risk tolerance, and establish, implement, and monitor appropriate risk management policies.
39. The NBFC must mitigate risks arising from inadequate system design and execution while implementing IT projects.
The NBFC must identify, document, and remediate system deficiencies and defects during the initial design, development, and testing phases.

40. The NBFC must establish a steering committee, consisting of business owners, the development team, and other stakeholders, to provide oversight and monitoring of the progress of the project, including deliverables to be realised at each phase of the project, and milestones to be reached according to the project timetable.
41. The NBFC must realign its IT systems on a regular basis in line with the changing needs of its customers and business.
For this purpose, the NBFC must have a board approved change management policy that encompasses the following: (1) prioritizing and responding to change proposals from business.
42. The Senior Management must be responsible to ensure that the Change Management policy is being followed on an ongoing basis.
43. The IT function of the NBFC must support a robust and comprehensive MIS in respect of various business functions as per the needs of the business and for supporting strategic decision-making.
44. The NBFC must put in place an MIS that assists the Senior Management as well as the business heads in decision making and to maintain an oversight over operations of various business verticals.

With robust IT systems in place, the NBFC must have the following (as per applicability) as part of an effective system-generated MIS (indicative list): (1) A dashboard for the Senior Management summarising financial position vis-à-vis targets.
It must include information such as trends of return on assets across categories, major growth business segments, and movement of net worth.
(3) The MIS must facilitate pricing of products, especially large ticket loans.
(4) The MIS must capture regulatory requirements and their compliance.
The regulatory requirement of reporting fraud to RBI must be system driven.
45. The NBFC must design and maintain its MIS keeping in view the prevailing supervisory reporting structure to facilitate generation of required information / returns for the supervisor.
46. The NBFC must ensure that all regulatory and supervisory returns are system-driven with seamless integration between the MIS and the supervisory reporting system.
The NBFC must provide ‘read-only’ access to RBI supervisors, to the MIS.

47. IS Audit must identify risks and methods to mitigate risk arising out of IT infrastructure such as server architecture, local and wide area networks, physical and information security, and telecommunications.
48. IS Audit must form an integral part of Internal Audit system of an NBFC.

While designing the IS Audit framework, an NBFC must refer to guidance issued by Professional bodies such as Information Systems Audit and Control Association (ISACA), Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA), and the Institute of Chartered Accountants (ICAI).
49. The NBFC must adopt an IS Audit framework duly approved by its Audit Committee of the Board (ACB).
50. The NBFC must have adequately skilled personnel in ACB who can understand the results of the IS Audit.
51. The IS Audit findings must be put up to the Board or ACB as per the NBFC’s IS Audit framework.

52. IS Audit must cover effectiveness of policy and oversight of IT systems, evaluate adequacy of processes and internal controls, and recommend corrective action to address deficiencies and follow-up.

59. BCP must be designed to minimise the operational, financial, legal, reputational, and other material consequences arising from a disaster.
The NBFC must have a Board approved BCP policy.
The functioning of BCP must be monitored by the Board by way of periodic reports.
The CIO must be responsible for formulation, review, and monitoring of BCP to ensure continued effectiveness.
The BCP must have the following salient features: (1).
The NBFC must first identify critical business verticals, locations, and shared resources to come up with the detailed Business Impact Analysis.
The process must envisage the impact of any unforeseen natural or man-made disasters on the NBFC’s business.
The NBFC must clearly list the business impact areas in order of priority.
The NBFC must fully understand the vulnerabilities associated with inter-relationships between various systems, departments, and business processes.

The NBFC must assess the probability of various failure scenarios under its BCP, evaluate available recovery options, and select the most cost-effective and practical strategy to minimise losses if a disaster.
(3) The NBFC must consider the need to put in place necessary backup sites for its critical business systems and data centres.

(4) The NBFC must test its BCP at least annually and whenever significant IT or business changes occur, to determine whether the entity can be restored to an acceptable level of operations within the timeframe specified in the contingency plan.
The NBFC must conduct the tests using worst-case scenarios and must place the test results and gap analysis before the CIO and the Board.
The NBFC must use the gap analysis and the Board’s observations as the basis for updating the BCP.
(5) The NBFC must ensure to put in place an appropriate mechanism to support testing of cyber resilience objectives among its vendors, service providers, and other relevant stakeholders.
